stories.shortLine: Waits for one opening. Makes it count.
stories.introduction: Sean grew up playing between the houses of San Fernando, where an afternoon match could hold up the walk home for hours. He helped assemble lantern frames after school and learned to notice the small mistake that throws a whole shape off. On court he is just as particular: one chosen angle, one committed run. Zack calls him slow. Sean keeps the score. His fire gets the crowd's attention, but the clean retrieval afterward is the part he wants them to remember.

stories.shortLine: Finds the angle before you see the opening.
stories.introduction: Zack learned tumbang preso on the roofdeck of his family's condo in Pasig. The court changed with laundry days, resident gatherings and whoever had claimed the shade, so he got good at finding an angle before anyone else settled in. Now he makes difficult plays look casual and casual plays unnecessarily difficult. Sean is usually the first to call him on it. Zack wants a national title, partly for himself and partly so the neighbours can say they used to beat him upstairs.

stories.shortLine: Holds the difficult space. Refuses to be rushed.
stories.introduction: In Montalban, Dante was the player trusted to keep a crowded game fair: settle the argument, straighten the can, give the youngest player another try. He still arrives early to mark out the plaza court. That patience becomes stubbornness when a rival tries to move him. His stone armour and shaking faults make the mountain stories he grew up hearing feel close enough to touch. Cheska admires his discipline. She also knows exactly how long he will defend a bad position.

stories.shortLine: Reads the space. Leaves you the harder route.
stories.introduction: Cheska grew up in La Trinidad and prefers the court before it gets noisy. She walks its edges, tests the footing and remembers where everyone likes to run. Friends mistake her quietness for caution until their easiest route freezes shut. Away from competition she is the practical one who remembered the water and checked the ride home. Losing bothers her more than she admits, especially when an untidy play works. Dante can make her wait; Zack can make her improvise. She is learning to enjoy both problems.

stories.shortLine: Looks distracted. Already knows your next move.
stories.introduction: Nemu grew up in Dumaguete, taking the long way home along the waterfront and stopping whenever a game had one place left. She seems to miss half the conversation, then remembers the detail everyone else forgot. Kuro has always been part of that routine: a curious little shadow at her shoulder, an alarming presence when a match turns serious. She refuses to explain him the same way twice. Phaister keeps trying to catch her by surprise. Nemu quietly saves those attempts for the walk home.

stories.shortLine: Sets the stage. Lets you discover the trick.
stories.introduction: Phaister grew up on Capul listening to stories about a moon that could disappear into a serpent's mouth. When she moved to Quezon City, she found a regular game beneath the rail line and an audience that was difficult to impress. That only made her more ambitious. She treats a match like a carefully timed reveal: invite a chase, leave a false opening, close the circle. The trouble is that she occasionally enjoys the setup more than winning. Nemu notices. Phaister wishes she would at least look surprised.

stories.shortLine: Fixes your slipper. Makes you guess his next throw.
stories.introduction: Rafi is an inventive boat-repairer and athlete from a fictional Sama Dilaut community in Tawi-Tawi. He notices the loose board, the awkward stair and the predictable opponent, then immediately has an idea. He repairs his own gear and keeps a small buoy token made from a useful offcut. He will help fix a rival's slipper strap, then bet that rival cannot read his next throw. His weakness is overplaying a clever idea when a simple shot would do. Sean's directness frustrates his elaborate feints; Cheska spots more of them than he likes. Tournament play is teaching him to make the useful choice, not merely the funny one. His water magic is his own.

stories.shortLine: Reads the wind. Gets there first.
stories.introduction: Amihan grew up in the rooms behind her family's loom in Vigan, where the cobbled street outside became a court whenever the kalesas stopped running. Cobbles send a slipper anywhere but straight, so she learned to throw with the wind, reading it off the abel hung out to air. She is bright, proud of her town and cannot stand a stalled game; when a match slows, she is the one pulling it back into motion. Sometimes she commits before the play is ready. Sean's patience drives her up the wall, and she tells Rafi his current goes nowhere without her wind.

Paete grew up as part of the forest on Mount Makiling. One wet season a woodcarver from Paete, across the lake, lost the trail in the mist, and Paete walked him down to the road; with nothing else to give, the carver cut the tree a face and it has worn the town's name ever since. At the forest's edge he found students playing tumbang preso and stood so still watching that they used him as the lata twice before he moved. Now he plays, unhurried and a little amused by everyone else's panic. He lets you take a run at anything. He just does not let you leave with it.
